sub_sections.title: Quality and effectiveness of the work plan, assessment of risks and appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages
sub_sections.content:
## 3.1 Quality and effectiveness of the work plan, assessment of risks and appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages

### Overall structure of the work plan

FIELDWISE is a single-researcher European Fellowship of 30 months, comprising a 24-month research and training programme at the beneficiary Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) (M1–M24) and a 6-month non-academic placement at AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság (M25–M30) under constraint CC-07. All research is executed by the experienced researcher, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, who carries every work package; the partner organisations contribute environment, data, supervision and evaluation in kind. The work plan is organised into five scientific work packages that form a single, deliberately linear evidence chain — from raw data and target definition, through physiological signal discovery and predictive modelling, to transferability testing and operational validation — plus a continuous cross-cutting strand of management, training and dissemination that spans the whole action.

The five work packages, with their leads and durations, are:

- **WP1 — Historical Data and Target Design** (M1–M6; lead: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem, contributing: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE)). Harmonises the five-year MATE hyperspectral, soil, meteorological and management archive, audits missingness and data quality, and — most importantly for the scientific claim — replaces spectral-proxy stress definitions with a physiologically grounded water-stress target and a leakage-safe validation design. Deliverables: **Harmonised historical database** (D1.1, M6), **Data/target/validation protocol** (D1.2, M6), and the **Career Development Plan** (D1.3, M3).
- **WP2 — Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer** (M3–M14; lead: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem, contributing: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE)). Discovers physiologically meaningful hyperspectral early-warning signatures and establishes their reproducibility in Sentinel-2-resampled spectral space. Deliverables: **Physiological validation dataset** (D2.1, M14) and **Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library** (D2.2, M14).
- **WP3 — Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction** (M6–M18; lead: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), contributing: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem). Develops calibrated, uncertainty-aware, multi-horizon forecasts, benchmarking transparent baselines, tree-ensemble and Bayesian/hierarchical approaches. Deliverables: **Comparative modelling benchmark** (D3.1, M18) and **FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card** (D3.2, M18).
- **WP4 — Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability** (M12–M21; lead: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem, contributing: Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив). Quantifies temporal (leave-one-year-out) transfer within the MATE data and Hungary-to-Bulgaria transfer to the independent MVCRI domain, and separates universal from site-specific predictors. Deliverables: **Temporal transferability benchmark** (D4.1, M21), **Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report** (D4.2, M21) and **Adaptation protocol** (D4.3, M21).
- **WP5 — Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP** (M16–M30; lead: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), contributing: AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság). Translates validated predictions into irrigation-priority logic and a functional web MVP, evaluates field-level decision value under commercial conditions, and defines a post-MSCA integration route. Deliverables: **DrR web MVP** (D5.1, M24), **Commercial-field transferability assessment** (D5.2, M30), **Field Decision Value report** (D5.3, M30), **AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation** (D5.4, M30) and **FMIS integration roadmap** (D5.5, M30).

Six milestones mark the verifiable transitions between phases: MS1 (M6, data and target readiness), MS2 (M12, a Sentinel-observable, physiologically meaningful early-warning signature established), MS3 (M16, the predictor ready for independent transferability testing), MS4 (M20, independent cross-country transferability quantified), MS5 (M23, the web MVP externally evaluated under farmer/operational conditions) and MS6 (M30, the non-academic placement completed from inside the host company). Each milestone attaches to a named deliverable and to a Steering Group go/no-go decision, so that no phase advances on the strength of an unverified predecessor.

### Timing of the work packages and their components

The schedule is designed so that dependencies are respected while overlap is exploited to keep the fellowship productive throughout. WP1 front-loads the data foundation in the first six months. WP2 begins at M3 and overlaps WP1, because signature discovery can start on the parts of the archive already harmonised; the WP1→WP2 relationship is a data dependency, not strict sequencing. WP3 opens at M6 (the month WP1 closes), consuming both the leakage-safe validation design fixed by task T1.5 and the Sentinel-compatible feature basis emerging from WP2. WP4 starts at M12: its early temporal-validation tasks run on interim models, while the hard dependency — zero-shot MATE→MVCRI transfer (T4.3) — is scheduled after the WP3 engine (D3.2) is available. WP5 begins at M16 and is the longest work package; the predictive engine is transferred into the MVP only after scientific validation, and the operational-transfer conclusions depend on the WP4 cross-country findings.

Deliverable due months follow this logic: D5.1 (the **DrR web MVP**) is deliberately dated M24, before the placement window opens, so that the M25–M30 placement is validation and transfer rather than first build. The one non-trivial sequencing question in the seed — D5.4 being claimed both by MS5 at M23 and by the placement window — is resolved in the finalised timeline by dating the **AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation** (D5.4) at M30 inside the placement and evidencing MS5 at M23 through the completed Field Decision Value assessment instead; the operational and interoperability assessment therefore belongs unambiguously to the placement and, together with the **FMIS integration roadmap** (D5.5), carries the MS6 verification.

Because this is a single-researcher action, the timeline is constrained so that concurrent work packages never demand more than one full-time equivalent of the fellow in any month; the finalised schedule closes with no unresolved scheduling constraints and no unresolved critical-path dependency. The critical path runs through the data foundation (T1.1, T1.4, MS1), the physiological-signal and modelling core (T2.2, T2.6, T3.4, T3.6, T3.7, MS3), the transferability adaptation (T4.6, MS4) and the operational transfer and placement (T5.4, T5.5, T5.6, MS6).

### Gantt chart (months elapsed)

The chart below shows work packages, the placement, the continuous management/training/dissemination strand, and the elapsed-month position of each major deliverable, milestone and Steering Group decision point. Columns are months 1–30 (months elapsed, not calendar dates); each cell is one month.

```
Month:                 1    5    10   15   20   25   30
                       |    |    |    |    |    |    |
WP1 Hist. Data/Target  ######........................
WP2 Phys. EW / H2S     ..############................
WP3 Prospective Pred.  .....#############............
WP4 Transferability    ...........##########.........
WP5 Oper./DrR MVP      ...............###############
Placement @ AgroVIR    ........................######
Mgmt/Training/Dissem.  ##############################

Milestones:   MS1(M6)  MS2(M12)  MS3(M16)  MS4(M20)  MS5(M23)  MS6(M30)
Deliverables: D1.3(M3); D1.1,D1.2(M6); D2.1,D2.2(M14); D3.1,D3.2(M18);
              D4.1,D4.2,D4.3(M21); D5.1(M24); D5.2,D5.3,D5.4,D5.5(M30)
Steering Group decision points: M6, M12, M16, M20, M27
Non-academic placement (secondment-equivalent): AgroVIR, M25-M30
```

The action contains one mobility event beyond the intersectoral placement: the fellow's incoming European-Fellowship move from Bulgaria to Hungary at the start of the action; there are no additional academic secondments in this single-beneficiary plan.

### Appropriateness of the effort assigned to the work packages

The fellow's effort totals 30.0 person-months, equal to the action duration, since the fellow is the only MSCA-funded effort. It is distributed as: WP1 3.0 PM (10.0%), WP2 5.5 PM (18.3%), WP3 5.5 PM (18.3%), WP4 4.0 PM (13.3%), WP5 9.0 PM (30.0%), and the cross-cutting management/training/dissemination strand 3.0 PM (10.0%). This profile is proportionate to scientific weight and risk: the two knowledge-generating work packages (WP2, WP3) together take 36.6% of effort, while WP5 is the single largest allocation because it carries the operational MVP, the commercial-field decision-value evidence, and the six-month evaluated placement. WP1 is intentionally lean but front-loaded, because a robust target definition and leakage-safe split are prerequisites for every downstream claim. The tightest month band is M16–M21, where WP4 and WP5 run concurrently; the timeline keeps this within one FTE.

Partner organisations contribute in-kind effort that is not funded or costed by MSCA-PF and therefore does not appear in the budget, but which substantiates the implementation narrative. The indicative in-kind estimates are: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem 2.4 PM (supervision, data preparation and experiment access); Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив 1.5 PM (WP4 trial hosting, ground and physiological measurement, and co-authorship of transfer-test outputs); AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság 3.0 PM (WP5 co-lead and placement host); and ELTE supervision of 2.5 PM (supervisor) and 2.0 PM (co-supervisor), giving an indicative partner in-kind total of 11.4 PM. These five figures are operator estimates to be confirmed with the partners; they are presented as indicative rather than committed, and the largest is deliberately AgroVIR's, as the only partner hosting the fellow. The co-supervisor, Dr. Roland Hollós, provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing, concentrated in the modelling-intensive window (WP3–WP4).

### Mechanisms to assess and mitigate risks

Risk is managed through a standing governance cadence and an explicit, itemised risk register. Oversight rests with a Project Steering Group chaired by the supervisor, Prof. András Jung, which meets at five corrective decision points — M6, M12, M16, M20 and M27 — and issues a go/no-go verdict at each milestone gate. The first four points align with MS1–MS4 and were introduced specifically to answer a prior evaluation criticism by embedding structured corrective moments; the fifth, at M27, is a mid-placement review that ensures the evaluated M25–M30 placement is not left unmonitored. During the placement the fellow works on site under a named AgroVIR on-site supervisor, indicatively Miklós Maróti at senior-research-officer grade; these placement-supervision details are working assumptions pending confirmation by the host company. A monthly written progress record and quarterly review against the Career Development Plan (D1.3) provide continuous, documented tracking between decision points.

The project maintains a 13-entry risk register (R01–R13) covering both research and administrative/technical risks, each with a likelihood, an impact and a concrete mitigation. Representative research risks include: incomplete historical MATE information (R01, medium/high — mitigated by a common-data subset, quality flags and prospective augmentation); a hyperspectral index with no Sentinel equivalent (R02 — retain for physiological discovery, exclude from the operational model); spectral and spatial mismatch between proximal and satellite sensing (R03, R04 — spectral-response-function resampling with concurrent sensor comparison, and representative plot/zone aggregation); too few physiological stress events (R05 — targeted temporal sampling across stress gradients); cloud gaps (R06 — temporal windows and Sentinel-1 where scientifically useful); and the transferability risks that unseen-year, Hungary-to-Bulgaria and farmer-field performance may drop (R07, R08, R09 — expected, quantified, and addressed by limited local/Bayesian adaptation and input/model simplification where necessary). A distinctive design risk, that a prediction may be accurate but arrive too late to act on (R11, medium/high), is mitigated by making lead time a primary model-selection criterion rather than an afterthought. Administrative and technical risks include web development delay (R12, low/medium — modular development building on the existing DrR prototype) and the possibility that full AgroVIR integration proves infeasible (R13, medium/medium — in which case the MVP assessment plus the integration roadmap remain a successful endpoint).

Underpinning the register is an explicit risk philosophy that de-risks the science itself: the failure of zero-shot transfer is not project failure. If FIELDWISE establishes that a model trained at MATE cannot reliably transfer to Bulgaria without a defined amount of local calibration, that quantified transferability gap is itself a significant scientific finding. This framing means the transferability work packages produce publishable, decision-relevant knowledge regardless of the sign of the result, and it is reinforced by the fallback endpoints written into R09, R10, R12 and R13, so that no single technical outcome can leave the fellowship without demonstrable results.

sub_sections.title: Quality and capacity of the host institutions and participating organisations, including hosting arrangements
sub_sections.content:
## 3.2 Quality and capacity of the host institutions and participating organisations, including hosting arrangements

### Structure of the action and applicability of the Global Fellowship provisions

FIELDWISE is a single-beneficiary MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship. The sole beneficiary and host organisation is Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), which carries the beneficiary obligations for the full 30 months of the action. FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship, built on the experienced researcher's intra-EU move from Bulgaria to Hungary; it therefore has no outgoing phase and no non-associated Third Country host, and the Global Fellowship requirement to outline both an outgoing Third Country host and a European return host does not apply to this proposal. Around the beneficiary, three participating organisations contribute environment, data, supervision and evaluation in kind: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem and Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив take part as associated partners, and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság takes part as the non-academic placement host for the M25–M30 window under constraint CC-07. The placement is an optional non-academic sector placement of the kind the call foresees and is presented here as an integral, evaluable element of the action, with its added value for the researcher's career development set out below and in §1.3. None of the participating organisations is a beneficiary; each is an entity the single-researcher work plan assigns activity to, and their infrastructure, logistics and facilities are detailed further in Part B-2 Section 5.

### Quality and capacity of the host institution — Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE)

The fellow is hosted in the Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), at H-1117 Budapest, Pázmány Péter sétány 1/C, and specifically within the institute's remote-sensing group, which is the interdisciplinary team the fellow joins. Supervision is deliberately interdisciplinary within the beneficiary itself: the co-supervisor sits in the ELTE Department of Meteorology, a different department from the hosting institute, so the beneficiary supplies both the geoinformatics/Earth-observation environment and the machine-learning and modelling expertise the work plan needs, without recourse to an external partner for either.

ELTE is the primary methodological and training environment of the action, covering geoinformatics, Earth observation, advanced and uncertainty-aware modelling, transferability analysis and research integration. Its GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratory provides the physical capability on which the physiological-signal and hyperspectral-to-Sentinel work depends: a DJI Matrice 350 RTK industrial drone with RTK GPS; DJI Zenmuse L1 (LiDAR and RGB), DJI Zenmuse P1 (45 MP photogrammetry) and DJI Zenmuse H20T (thermal, zoom, wide) payloads; an Ultris S5 hyperspectral camera covering the VIS–NIR narrow bands; and a Cubert CUVIS Lab Lite hyperspectral-imaging package with calibration tools. The Ultris S5 and the Cubert CUVIS are the institute's own hyperspectral capability and are the instruments the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel resampling in WP2 relies on. On the software and computation side the laboratory offers licensed ArcGIS, ENVI and MATLAB alongside Google Earth Engine, QGIS, SNAP, Python and R, high-performance computing clusters for AI and large-scale geospatial analysis, and secure storage and backup for large remote-sensing datasets, complemented by ELTE library, IT services and open-science repositories. This inventory is a current snapshot maintained by the institute and covers every computational and sensing resource the work plan calls on.

The scientific standing of the hosting group is evidenced by its recent output, taken from the publication record of the supervisor, Prof. András Jung: Szabó, Jung, Varga, Hajdú, Revoly, Lausch, Vohland and Sipos (2025), Agronomy 15(12), 2860; Kundathil, Varga, Szalay, Sipos and Jung (2025), Applied Sciences 15(22), 12254; Lausch, Bumberger, Jung, Pause, Selsam, Zhou and Herzog (2025), Agriculture 15(21), 2233; and Lin, Jing, Li and Jung (2024), IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters 21. The three 2025 items are Earth-observation and agricultural-monitoring work that is directly adjacent to the crop-monitoring methods FIELDWISE uses; the 2024 letter evidences deep-learning method breadth. FIELDWISE claims this record as adjacency and demonstrated capability in EO for agriculture rather than as identical prior work on crop-stress prediction.

Supervision is provided by two named ELTE staff and no others. The supervisor, Prof. András Jung, is a Professor at the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics working in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, geospatial technologies and environmental monitoring; he chairs the Project Steering Group and is the escalation point in the supervision structure. The co-supervisor, Dr. Roland Hollós, of the ELTE Department of Meteorology, works on machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and on agro-meteorology, and provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing across WP3 and WP4; the fellow designs, builds and runs the models, while the co-supervisor quality-assures them. The mentoring cadence that binds this structure — weekly one-to-ones with the supervisor, weekly technical sessions with the co-supervisor through the modelling-intensive window and quarterly review against the Career Development Plan — is set out in §3.1 and is not repeated here.

Honesty about hosting history is material to the evaluation. ELTE has not previously hosted a funded MSCA fellow. It has, however, hosted an MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship application with the same fellow and the same supervisor — PLANTDIGISENSE (HORIZON-MSCA-2025-PF, proposal 101284764), which scored 70.40% against a 70.00 threshold — so the institution has demonstrably prepared to host this researcher and this project before, and FIELDWISE is a considered resubmission rather than a first, untested pairing. This is stated as an application record and an established supervisory relationship, not as prior funded-hosting experience the institution does not have.

### Hosting arrangements, integration and support services

The hosting arrangements ELTE provides for the fellow are: a dedicated office and laboratory space at ELTE; full integration into the institute's research groups, with weekly meetings and interdisciplinary workshops; administrative and technical support for relocation, project management, procurement and dissemination; access to short-term training courses; and participation in international networks (COST Actions, and FAO and EU webinars). These arrangements were established for the same applicant, host, institute and supervisor and are institutional facts about how ELTE integrates and supports an incoming fellow. Integration is reinforced by a genuinely bidirectional knowledge exchange, described in §1.3: ELTE transfers geoinformatics, EO time-series analysis, hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer, spatio-temporal and Bayesian hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning and reproducible geospatial computation to the fellow, while the fellow brings plant physiology, horticultural crop science, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping and the biological interpretation of Earth observation into the hosting group. ELTE remains the beneficiary and the fellow's home institution across the whole 30-month action, including during the M25–M30 non-academic placement, which is an intersectoral extension of the European Fellowship rather than a change of host.

### Quality and capacity of the participating organisations

**Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem — primary experimental and data environment (associated partner).** Through its Institute of Horticultural Sciences, Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem supplies the five-year source-domain dataset, the processing-tomato experimental environment, the hyperspectral, soil and weather information and the primary scientific validation on which model development rests; it is the source domain for the WP4 transfer test. Its scientific capacity is the best-evidenced of the three participating organisations: it coordinates the AGRIGEP project (grant 101094158, verified on CORDIS), and the Institute of Horticultural Sciences has recent, directly relevant publications, including Takács, Helyes, Ilahy, Daood and Pék (2026, Smart Agricultural Technology 15) on predicting water-stress-related traits in open-field tomato — the same crop and stress as FIELDWISE — together with Silva e Souza et al. (2026, Horticulturae 12(7), 896) and Kuchár et al. (2026, Agronomy 16(8), 844). The organisational contact and the partner's representative on the Steering Group is Dr. Sándor Takács of the Institute of Horticultural Sciences, who is an author on all three of those publications, so the source-domain claim is anchored on evidence rather than on assertion. In addition, Prof. Gábor Milics — a full professor at Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem in Gödöllő, Hungary's country representative to the International Society of Precision Agriculture and a specialist in remote sensing for precision agriculture — advises the fellow personally, adding a second scientific-advisory strand outside the formal governance structure.

**Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив — cross-country transferability environment (associated partner).** Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив (MVCRI) is a public research institute of the Bulgarian Agricultural Academy and provides the independent Bulgarian processing-tomato environment required for cross-country scientific transferability; its role is specifically the Hungary→Bulgaria transfer test rather than a simple increase in sample size. The relevant department is Technologies in Vegetable Crops Production, headed by Prof. Vinelina Yankova (entomology, vegetable production and breeding), whose remit is precisely the one the WP4 Bulgarian transfer test sits within; a second department, Breeding, Variety Maintenance and Introduction, is headed by Assoc. Prof. Stanislava Grozeva. Prof. Vinelina Yankova is the partner's contact and its seat on the Steering Group. The institute's recent record includes coordination of FP7 grant 205941 in its own name (verified on CORDIS), a current Agricultural Academy task (ZEMDKT 17, 2024–2026) on resistance to abiotic stress — drought and salinity — in Solanum lycopersicum, the same crop and stress as FIELDWISE, and a National Science Fund project (KP-06-COST/2, 2025-ongoing) on satellite and UAV monitoring of vegetable crops with the Space Research and Technology Institute of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences under COST Action PANGEOS. Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив is also the fellow's current employer of record; the transfer test is deliberately not answerable to the fellow whose model it tests, and its contact and steering seat are held by a department head rather than by the fellow, so the cross-country evaluation remains independent.

**AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság — operational and farmer-field evaluator, and non-academic placement host.** AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság (AgroVIR) is a Hungarian SME founded in 2007 and seated in Budaörs; it develops and operates a cloud-based farm management information system (FMIS) built on twenty years of practice in Hungarian commercial agriculture, in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries — Hungary, Romania, Azerbaijan, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Serbia, Ukraine and Argentina — with the Hungarian and Bulgarian footprints matching the two countries FIELDWISE works in. This commercial-scale operating environment is what WP5 uses to test research-to-farm transferability. The company is registered under NACE 7020 (business and management consulting), reflecting its founding activity, while its current business is agricultural software; its company registration number is 13-09-200433. AgroVIR provides network access to the AgroVIR platform and its commercial farm base and validation of the prediction pipeline through the AgroVIR software. Its relevant track record is commercial rather than scientific: AgroVIR has not participated in EU-funded research projects, and FIELDWISE relies on its production-scale commercial deployment, not on a research-collaboration history it does not have. The partner's project contact and its Steering Group seat are held by Zsuzsanna Balázs. Consistent with the 2026 Guide for Applicants, no letter of commitment is included for the non-academic placement host, and its absence is not a weakness; the placement is nonetheless fully evaluated on the argument below.

### Hosting arrangements for the non-academic placement (AgroVIR, M25–M30)

The six-month non-academic placement at AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság is designed to give the fellow an experience the beneficiary cannot provide, and the proposal is explicit about who supervises her, where she works, what she does and what she gains. On site she is supervised by Miklós Maróti; his grade is that of a senior research officer, i.e. a research-side supervisor rather than a purely commercial engineering post, which is the register the placement's training rationale needs. She is provided with desk or office space at AgroVIR for the M25–M30 window, access to the FMIS development and staging environment, and access to the customer-data environment; on the basis of that access and the work content she is embedded in the AgroVIR product development team responsible for the FMIS platform, reporting to the on-site placement supervisor. Her six-month work programme comprises four items that deepen existing WP5 content rather than open a new strand: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment that produces the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4, M30); the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company, which produces the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5, M30); and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. What the placement offers that ELTE cannot is a production FMIS environment, a commercial engineering practice and direct contact with paying growers — none of which the beneficiary, as a methodological and training environment with research infrastructure, can supply. Separately from the placement, AgroVIR also provides field trials with farmers via its network from M16 in its capacity as the operational evaluator; that field access exists independently of the placement and is not counted as placement workspace.

### Involvement of participating organisations and associated-partner arrangements

Each participating organisation contributes in kind and holds a named seat on the Project Steering Group described in §3.1: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem through Dr. Sándor Takács, Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив through Prof. Vinelina Yankova, and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság through Zsuzsanna Balázs. Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem and Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив participate as associated partners, and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság participates as the non-academic placement host; together they form a coherent academic-research-to-industry chain — source scientific environment, independent cross-country environment and operational commercial environment — that mirrors the validation ladder of the action, with the sole beneficiary ELTE providing the methodological and training core. Several placement-host descriptors (the on-site supervisor and his grade, the workspace and system access, the identity of the team the fellow joins, and the AgroVIR contact's role) rest on descriptions supplied for, but not yet formally confirmed by, the participating organisations, and will be confirmed with the partners before submission.

WP1, WP2 and WP4 are led by Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (DATA_PARTNER); WP3 and WP5 are led by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) (HOST).
Work-package durations are WP1 M1-M6, WP2 M3-M14, WP3 M6-M18, WP4 M12-M21, WP5 M16-M30.
Deliverable due months: D1.3 M3; D1.1 and D1.2 M6; D2.1 and D2.2 M14; D3.1 and D3.2 M18; D4.1, D4.2 and D4.3 M21; D5.1 M24; D5.2, D5.3, D5.4 and D5.5 M30, with canonical titles.
Milestones MS1 (M6), MS2 (M12), MS3 (M16), MS4 (M20) and MS5 (M23) with their criteria.
MS6 at M30 marks completion of the non-academic placement and is carried by deliverables D5.4 and D5.5.
Task-level month allocations and the critical path (T1.1, T1.4, MS1, T2.2, T2.6, T3.4, T3.6, T3.7, MS3, T4.6, MS4, T5.4, T5.5, T5.6, MS6) as finalised in the Gantt.
D5.4 is dated M30 within the placement window and MS5 at M23 is evidenced by the completed Field Decision Value assessment, resolving the D5.4 double-claim.
As a single-researcher action the fellow executes all work packages, concurrent work packages stay within one FTE per month, and the finalised schedule has no unresolved scheduling constraints.
The fellow's effort totals 30.0 person-months: WP1 3.0, WP2 5.5, WP3 5.5, WP4 4.0, WP5 9.0, cross-cutting 3.0.

The six-month placement work programme is four items: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4, M30); the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5, M30) written from inside the implementing company; and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers.
The placement offers a production FMIS environment, commercial engineering practice and direct grower contact that ELTE, as a methodological/training environment, cannot supply.
AgroVIR also provides field trials with farmers via its network from M16 as the operational evaluator, independently of the placement and not counted as placement workspace.
